_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: Austin directed new parks security equipment while adding an AI restriction. That resolution also points back to the city's broader surveillance review and privacy requirements.

introduction.text: Austin's parks security resolution authorizes a plan and equipment, but it is not an unrestricted technology purchase. The [adopted measure](c6) names potential equipment and requires compliance with the city's existing surveillance ordinance.

The city manager may not consider buying a camera or drone system that depends on AI for surveillance or analysis. That specific prohibition sits alongside the separate approval and privacy process the resolution incorporates.

paragraphs.text: The city manager must use the parks department's security audit to develop the implementation plan. It must identify improvements, priority locations, responsible parties, funding and timelines. Parks with a history of violent crime receive priority for initial deployment.

The [surveillance ordinance](c16) requires a privacy impact assessment for technology a department seeks to acquire. The assessment must be public when delivered to the council. The chapter also specifies exceptions to its ordinary approval requirement.

Potential use of collected data to train AI is part of that risk assessment. It weighs against a finding of minimal privacy risk. That factor is distinct from the ordinance's separate list of prohibited technologies and its policy exceptions.

The council's action notes mark the item approved but publish no vote count beside it. They say vote details will appear in approved minutes. The available record supports approval, not a tally supplied by inference.
